articles.summary: By Molly Tripp, Director of Programs and Contracts In mission-critical environments, a failed component is rarely the biggest problem. The real costs come from delayed missions, production interruptions, maintenance burdens, supply chain disruptions, and the operational uncertainty that follows. For defense and industrial programs, maintaining availability requires more than reliable technology. It requires a proactive lifecycle management strategy. At One Stop Systems (OSS), we help customers stay ahead of downtime through disciplined configuration management, proactive obsolescence monitoring, supply chain risk mitigation, and long-term sustainment planning that protects operational readiness throughout the life of a program. When Availability Becomes the Mission For many organizations, system performance traditionally centers on speed, processing power, or functionality. However, in mission-critical applications, availability often matters just as much as capability. A highly capable system that is unavailable when needed can quickly become a liability. Defense platforms operating in remote environments, industrial control systems managing production lines, and critical communications networks all depend on consistent uptime to fulfill their intended mission. Even a short outage can trigger cascading consequences: Delayed operations and mission objectives Production interruptions and lost output Increased labor costs for troubleshooting and recovery Reduced confidence among operators and stakeholders Elevated safety and compliance risks As a result, organizations are increasingly evaluating technologies not only for what they can do, but for how reliably they can perform throughout their operational lifecycle. OSS has extensive experience applying these principles across both military and commercial programs, helping customers improve system availability, reduce lifecycle risk, and maintain mission readiness in some of the world's most demanding operational environments. From defense applications such as C5ISR, sensor fusion, autonomy, and missile defense systems to commercial deployments in robotics, medical, aerospace, mining, and industrial markets, OSS solutions are designed to deliver reliable operation in environments where uptime is critical. The Real Impact of Repair and Replacement Delays When a critical component fails, restoring functionality is rarely as simple as installing a replacement. During conversations with defense and industrial customers, one challenge comes up repeatedly: the cost of a failure is rarely limited to replacing the failed component. More often, the greatest impact comes from the labor required to diagnose the issue, coordinate replacement parts, validate system performance, and return the platform to service. These indirect costs often exceed the cost of the hardware itself. This is especially true in applications operating in remote locations or military environments, where any change that is not form-fit-function (FFF) compatible may require years of planning, budgeting, program approval, funding allocation, engineering updates, and successful completion of design verification testing (DVT) before implementation. At OSS, we have seen these challenges impact aircraft, submarines, data centers, and other mission-critical platforms. These experiences have reinforced the importance of designing systems with long-term availability, maintainability, and lifecycle management in mind. This philosophy is embodied in solutions such as the OSS 3U SDS Gen5, a rugged enterprise-class compute and storage platform designed for demanding environments where uptime and lifecycle support are critical to mission success. Many mission-critical systems operate in environments where maintenance windows are limited, access is restricted, or equipment is geographically dispersed. In these situations, the time required to diagnose, ship, replace, and validate a failed component can significantly extend system downtime. The costs associated with delayed repairs often include: Extended operational disruption Additional maintenance personnel hours Increased inventory carrying costs Deployment schedule impacts Customer contractual penalties In defense and industrial applications, replacement timelines measured in weeks or months can have substantial operational consequences. This reality places greater emphasis on selecting technologies that are designed for reliability from the outset and supported throughout their lifecycle. Supply Chain Resilience Matters More Than Ever The past several years have highlighted how vulnerable global supply chains can be to disruption. According to the U.S. Department of Defense Industrial Capabilities Reports, supply chain fragility continues to present significant risks to defense readiness. Component shortages, transportation delays, geopolitical uncertainty, and shifting manufacturing priorities have all contributed to extended lead times across multiple industries. For mission-critical systems, these challenges introduce additional risk. Organizations must consider questions such as: Are replacement components readily available? How long will the technology be supported? Are there multiple qualified sources for critical parts? What happens if a component becomes obsolete? A failure may be manageable if a replacement is available within days. The same failure can become a major operational event if replacement parts are unavailable for months. We've seen organizations spend months solving a reliability issue only to discover the replacement component is no longer available or has a lead time that stretches into the next budget cycle. That experience has pushed many program teams to evaluate supply chain resilience much earlier in the design process. These challenges highlight a larger reality: maintaining system availability begins long before a failure occurs. It starts during the design and planning phases of a program and OSS can help. How OSS Helps Customers Maintain Long-Term System Availability One of the most overlooked contributors to uptime is lifecycle planning. Throughout my career supporting defense and industrial programs, I've found that the organizations with the highest system availability are usually the ones that started planning for lifecycle support long before the first unit was deployed. Many systems are deployed with a focus on immediate performance requirements, while long-term maintainability receives less attention. However, mission-critical platforms often remain in service for years or even decades, making lifecycle support a critical factor in total cost of ownership. Lifecycle-focused design considerations include: Long-term component availability Upgrade pathways Serviceability and maintainability Documentation and technical support Configuration management Obsolescence planning Organizations that address these factors during the design phase are often better positioned to avoid costly surprises later in the system's operational life. Rather than reacting to failures after they occur, lifecycle planning enables a more proactive approach to reliability and availability management. OSS offers lifecycle management for this exact reason, and our experience across defense and commercial programs has consistently demonstrated the value of proactive lifecycle planning in improving long-term system availability. Why Ruggedization Is About More Than Durability Ruggedization is frequently viewed as a feature designed to withstand harsh environments. While environmental protection remains important, its value extends far beyond simple durability. Mission-critical systems routinely encounter: Extreme temperatures Vibration and shock Dust and contaminants Moisture and humidity Electromagnetic interference Continuous operation demands These conditions accelerate wear and increase the likelihood of failure for components not designed to withstand them. The consequence is not merely equipment damage. It is operational disruption, maintenance expense, and reduced availability. Effective ruggedization, like OSS provides, helps reduce unexpected failures by ensuring systems can perform reliably in the environments where they are actually deployed. In many applications, ruggedization serves as a preventative measure that directly contributes to uptime and long-term operational readiness. Learn more about our defense-focused rugged edge computing solutions on our Defense page. The Business Case for Reliability Downtime is often treated as a maintenance issue. In reality, it is a business issue. Every hour of unplanned downtime can affect productivity, budgets, schedules, customer confidence, and mission success. Research from Uptime Institute continues to show that outages can carry significant financial consequences, with more than half of surveyed organizations reporting that their most recent major outage cost over $100,000 and approximately one in five reporting losses exceeding $1 million. While organizations naturally focus on acquisition costs during procurement, the larger financial impact frequently emerges after deployment through maintenance requirements, repair delays, and operational interruptions. Program managers, operators, and procurement teams are increasingly evaluating reliability not as a technical feature, but as a factor that directly affects budgets, schedules, and operational readiness. By prioritizing system availability, planning for lifecycle support, managing supply chain risk, and investing in technologies designed for demanding environments, organizations can significantly reduce the hidden costs associated with downtime. OSS additionally provides an additional set of eyes on the health of your system with advanced management technologies. Our U-BMC platform provides proactive monitoring, diagnostics, and system-health visibility that help organizations identify issues before they result in operational disruption. Looking Beyond the Initial Purchase In mission-critical environments, the question is not whether failures will occur, but how prepared an organization is to minimize their impact. Technology decisions made today influence operational readiness for years to come. Evaluating solutions through the lens of availability, maintainability, supply chain resilience, and lifecycle support helps organizations move beyond short-term purchasing decisions and focus on long-term mission success. In the field, users rarely talk about specifications once a system has been deployed. What they remember is whether the system was available when they needed it most. Consistent performance over time is what ultimately determines mission success. This is where OSS can support your application to make sure your deployment achieves and maintains the highest level of availability. How One Stop Systems Helps Reduce Downtime Risk The organizations that achieve the highest levels of operational readiness are often those that take a proactive approach to availability rather than reacting to failures after they occur. Minimizing downtime requires more than selecting reliable technology. It requires planning for the realities that affect every deployed system, from harsh operating conditions and component obsolescence to supply chain disruptions and unexpected field failures. At One Stop Systems (OSS), we help customers address these challenges through ruggedized edge computing platforms, proactive system management capabilities, disciplined configuration management, obsolescence planning, and long-term lifecycle support. By proactively addressing obsolescence, environmental challenges, and supply chain risks, OSS helps customers maximize availability and mission readiness throughout the lifecycle of their systems.

articles.summary: OSS technology qualified for leading enterprise server platform, expanding access to new commercial and datacenter customers and markets Integrated solution enables enterprise customers to accelerate AI adoption while leveraging existing technology infrastructure ESCONDIDO, Calif. – October 26, 2026 – One Stop Systems, Inc. (OSS or the Company) (Nasdaq: OSS), a leader in high-performance compute and PCIe expansion solutions for artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and demanding edge applications, announced today that its flagship Gen5 4UP-MAX expansion system has been qualified for use with a tier 1 global enterprise computing platform provider, expanding the Company's addressable market and creating new opportunities to support enterprise AI adoption broadly across commercial and datacenter applications. The qualification represents an important milestone in OSS's strategy to expand its presence in the enterprise AI market, making its high-performance computing technology available to organizations seeking to integrate advanced AI capabilities into their existing infrastructure. As businesses move beyond AI experimentation toward broader deployment, demand is growing for computing solutions that can handle increasingly complex workloads while preserving existing technology investments. OSS's technology addresses this need by enabling enterprise customers to add substantial AI processing capacity to their existing computing environments without the need to replace their core server systems. Mike Knowles, President and CEO of OSS, said, “This qualification represents an important milestone for OSS and further validates the value of our high-performance computing technology in addressing the rapidly evolving needs of the enterprise AI market. By making our technology available through an established global computing ecosystem, we are expanding our reach into new markets and creating opportunities to support a broader base of enterprise, commercial, and datacenter customers. We believe this development reinforces our strategy to leverage our core technical capabilities across multiple high-growth AI markets.” At the center of the solution is OSS's Gen5 4UP-MAX expansion system, which enables enterprise customers to integrate up to eight high-performance, 675W AI accelerators from leading manufacturers directly into their existing server infrastructure, with the flexibility to scale computing capacity by connecting multiple expansion systems to a single server. Designed to support demanding AI workloads, including model training, fine-tuning, and inference, the platform combines substantial computing capacity with advanced data center management capabilities through OSS's U-BMC technology, providing enhanced system monitoring and control. The solution also supports confidential computing, helping protect sensitive data during AI processing. Advanced power and cooling architectures are designed to support sustained performance under demanding AI workloads. Combined, these capabilities provide organizations with a scalable, secure, and manageable approach to expanding AI computing performance. Jim Ison, Chief Product Officer of OSS, said, “As enterprises move from experimenting with AI to deploying it across their operations, they need solutions that deliver greater computing power without sacrificing security, reliability, or manageability. Our solution addresses these requirements by combining exceptional processing capacity with the flexibility to scale as customer needs evolve. By integrating high-density acceleration, advanced system management, and purpose-built power and cooling capabilities, we provide a differentiated solution for increasingly demanding enterprise AI applications. This is particularly important for organizations looking to accelerate AI adoption while maximizing their existing infrastructure investments.” About One Stop SystemsOne Stop Systems, Inc. (Nasdaq: OSS) is a leader in AI enabled solutions for the demanding 'edge'. OSS designs and manufactures Enterprise Class compute and storage products that enable rugged AI, sensor fusion and autonomous capabilities without compromise. These hardware and software platforms bring the latest data center performance to harsh and challenging applications, whether they are on land, sea or in the air. OSS products include ruggedized servers, compute accelerators, flash storage arrays, and storage acceleration software. These specialized compact products are used across multiple industries and applications, including autonomous trucking and farming, as well as aircraft, drones, ships and vehicles within the defense industry. OSS solutions address the overall AI workflow, from high-speed data acquisition to deep learning, training and large-scale inference, and have delivered many industry firsts for industrial OEM and government customers. As one of the fastest growing segments of the multi-billion-dollar edge computing market, AI enabled solutions require-and OSS delivers-the highest level of performance in the most challenging environments without compromise. OSS products are available directly or through global distributors. For more information, go to www.onestopsystems.com. You can also follow OSS on X, YouTube, and LinkedIn. articles.summary: Real-time inference faces a familiar operations problem: keep work moving through constrained stages. The solution may be a faster conveyor, another parallel path, or fewer unnecessary handoffs—not simply a faster processor. By Braden Cooper, Director of Products Section 1: Why Treat Real-Time Edge AI Like a Factory Floor? A real-time Edge AI pipeline behaves like a factory floor: data enters as demand, moves through constrained processing stages, waits when capacity falls short, and exits as detections, tracking vectors, or actuation commands. When one stage cannot keep pace, queues grow—and throughput, response time, and deterministic control suffer. The technology is different, but the flow problem is familiar: demand can exceed capacity, work can accumulate between stages, and one constrained resource can limit the entire system. That is why operations management provides a useful framework for Edge AI optimization. Bottleneck analysis, Little’s Law, demand distributions, and queuing theory apply here just as they do on a production line. They let us put numbers behind the traffic jam and decide what to change. Model and compute benchmarks matter, but they do not describe performance under real mission demand. A fast model cannot sustain its rated inference throughput when host-memory copies, interconnect contention, limited buffer capacity, or competing workloads delay the data it needs. The practical shift is from tuning components in isolation to optimizing the complete flow. That begins by mapping the pipeline and finding the constraint that governs end-to-end performance. At OSS, we use this framework to evaluate rugged Edge AI platforms as complete data pipelines. PCIe interconnects, switch fabrics, GPU and NVMe connectivity, scheduling, and thermal architecture must work together to sustain flow—not just deliver isolated benchmark results. Figure 1. Sensor demand moves through shared data paths, buffers, and GPU processing stages, exposing the constraints that govern completed inference throughput. Section 2: How Do You Map a Real-Time Edge AI Pipeline? Consider a laser-weeding system moving through a field. Cameras and LIDAR scan the plants ahead, AI determines which plants are weeds, and the machine directs a laser to the right location—all while the vehicle continues moving. The decision must arrive within a predictable time window. A delayed result is not merely slower computing; it can mean treating the wrong spot or missing the weed entirely. To model that workflow, begin with a network diagram: a map of the stages the data must pass through and the connections between them. Each stage performs useful work, has finite capacity, and can create a queue when demand arrives faster than it can be served. In factory terms, the sensor data is the incoming material, the connections are conveyors, memory is work-in-process storage, processors are work centers, and the weed classification and targeting command are the finished output. 1. Capture — the receiving dock. Cameras, LIDAR, and other sensors observe the crop row. An FPGA can collect and organize these high-speed inputs close to the sensors so the rest of the system receives data in a predictable form. 2. Homogenize — inspection and preparation. Software or dedicated hardware aligns timestamps, converts formats, filters noise, and combines sensor feeds. This turns several different input streams into a consistent set of frames or objects that the AI can use. 3. Transport — the conveyor system. The prepared data must reach GPU memory or high-speed storage. A direct PCIe path can avoid unnecessary trips through CPU memory, reducing processor overhead and traffic across shared processor interconnects such as QPI or UPI. 4A. Local inference — an on-site work center. The prepared data stays on the machine and moves across PCIe into a local GPU or inference accelerator. The result then travels directly to the laser-control system. 4B. Cloud inference — an external work center. Alternatively, selected data can be packaged for transmission through a NIC and 5G modem, sent across the mobile network to a cloud inference accelerator, processed remotely, and returned as a targeting decision. This branch adds an outbound transfer, network transit, cloud queue and processing time, and a return transfer before the machine can act. 5. Communicate, actuate, or store — shipping and records. A local result can be sent to the laser-control system, recorded to storage, or transmitted through a NIC to another system. For the cloud branch, the returned decision must move from the 5G modem through the control path before the laser can fire. These outbound and return paths consume bandwidth and add service time. 6. Software transport layers — the dispatch rules. Drivers, messaging frameworks, data-movement libraries, schedulers, network protocols, and cloud services coordinate the handoffs between stages. They determine what data is sent, what stays local, where work waits, and how much copying or retransmission occurs. Once the stages are visible, three practical constraints usually stand out: Sensor-ingest capacity: Multiple cameras and LIDAR feeds can produce data faster than the FPGA, Ethernet link, or switched fabric can accept it. The first queue forms before the AI sees a frame. CPU and system-memory staging: If each frame is first copied into CPU memory, prepared there, and then copied again to GPU memory, the CPU becomes an unnecessary handling station. The extra movement consumes memory bandwidth, processor time, and capacity on shared CPU interconnects such as QPI or UPI. PCIe path contention: Cameras, FPGA cards, GPUs, storage, and NICs may share PCIe lanes or a common switch uplink. Even when each device is fast on its own, the shared path can become the factory conveyor that limits the entire line. The design objective is to shorten and balance this path. Where the hardware and software stack support it, direct or peer-to-peer data movement can place prepared sensor data closer to GPU-accessible memory without unnecessary CPU staging. The benefit is not “zero copy” as a slogan; it is fewer handoffs, less traffic through constrained resources, and more predictable time from observation to laser command. The network diagram also makes measurement straightforward. At each stage, record the incoming data rate, effective service capacity, queue or buffer depth, and processing time. For local inference, follow the route through the FPGA, PCIe switches, GPU, storage, and laser controller. For cloud inference, also measure payload size, uplink and downlink capacity, network round-trip time, cloud queue time, remote processing time, and the variability of each interval. The path with the least remaining capacity—or the longest persistent queue—becomes the likely system constraint. Measure both paths against the same demand, capacity, handoffs, and end-to-end flow time. Throughput and delay then tell us how much work stays in flight, how much buffering it needs, and how often the system can meet the laser-control deadline. Figure 2. Local and cloud inference branches share sensor capture and preparation but introduce different transport, queueing, processing, and control-path constraints. Section 3: How Do Bandwidth and Latency Dictate Edge AI Memory? Bandwidth keeps up with arriving work. Latency determines whether that work finishes in time to matter. Think conveyor width versus transit time: we need enough of both to get from a sensor observation to a laser command before the machine passes the plant. Start with 48 cameras, each delivering an approximately 8 MB uncompressed image at 120 frames/s after FPGA processing and format conversion. For scale, a 3840 × 2160 image at one byte per pixel contains approximately 8.29 MB. Synchronize those 48 prepared frames and we have a 384 MB package arriving every 8.33 milliseconds. Send each complete package across the PCIe x16 path once, and the math is straightforward: 384 MB/package × 120 packages/s = 46.08 GB/s. That is before LIDAR or any other traffic joins the line. That workload devours bandwidth. A Gen5 x16 path with 52 GB/s of usable capacity runs at 88.6% utilization and takes approximately 7.38 milliseconds/package in serialization delay—the time spent transferring the package over the link. Move to Gen6 x16 at 104 GB/s and utilization drops to 44.3%, while serialization delay falls to approximately 3.69 milliseconds/package. We get a shorter transfer and more breathing room. Another option is to add an independent conveyor and dispatch work across both rather than move each lot faster. The multi-accelerator pool must handle 5,760 camera frames/s: 48 cameras at 120 frames/s, not 120 individual frames/s. Model the multi-GPU array as one aggregate work center that processes a complete package in 6 milliseconds, providing approximately 167 complete packages/s. At 120 packages/s, inference uses 72% of that capacity. Batch size, data placement, and tensor pre-processing determine how the work and latency are distributed across individual GPUs. Allow another 4 milliseconds for capture, preparation, queueing, and control, excluding PCIe transfer. Hold that allowance constant and add the 6 milliseconds of processing: sensor-to-command flow time comes to approximately 17.38 milliseconds with Gen5 or 13.69 milliseconds with Gen6. Successive packages overlap across stages, just as different lots move through different factory work centers at the same time. Little’s Law — stable-pipeline averagesAverage WIP = Average Throughput × Average Flow TimeWIP is measured in packages, throughput in packages per second, and flow time in seconds. For a hard real-time sensor design built around ping-pong double buffering—such as 360-degree situational awareness or robotics—the strict operational target is L < 2, or Work-In-Process < 2, with L representing average WIP. Two occupied buffers represent the familiar overlap: one frame transferring while the previous frame is processing. Under this two-buffer constraint, sustained L > 2 means the required work in flight exceeds the available slots. With continuous, fixed-rate video arrivals and no spare service capacity to drain the backlog, work queues and the system cannot catch up without dropping frames. Work-in-process, or WIP, is everything that has entered the pipeline but has not yet produced a command—including work being transferred or processed, not just work waiting in a queue. A fractional average does not mean a fractional package exists at one instant; it means the number in flight varies over time. Applying Little’s LawGen5: 120 packages/s × 0.01738 s ≈ 2.09 packagesGen6: 120 packages/s × 0.01369 s ≈ 1.64 packages Gen5 (L = 2.09) breaches the double-buffer threshold and forces queueing. Gen6 (L = 1.64) stays safely inside the L < 2 limit to preserve deterministic timing. That is the architectural advantage—not just a faster transfer, but less work tied up between observation and command. At 384 MB per package, this represents approximately 801 MB of input-equivalent WIP with Gen5 or 631 MB with Gen6. The faster conveyor reduces transfer time and material in flight. Physical buffers must also accommodate intermediate tensors, copies, and arrival bursts: average WIP is a starting point, not the final memory budget. Cloud Bandwidth — The External Shipping Lane The cloud path hits a much narrower shipping lane. Sending the full array requires 46.08 GB/s = 368.64 Gb/s before networking overhead—3,072 times the assumed 120 Mb/s usable uplink. Even reducing every camera frame to 100 kB leaves us with 5,760 frames/s × 100 kB = 576 MB/s = 4.608 Gb/s, still 38.4 times the uplink’s capacity. The machine has to select regions, features, or events locally before the external work center can keep up. Instead, let local processing select one 100 kB request from each complete 384 MB package. Now the uplink carries 120 requests/s × 100 kB = 12 MB/s = 96 Mb/s, using 80% of the assumed 120 Mb/s usable capacity. That fits, but it changes the division of work. The cloud handles a selected downstream task; the machine still does significant processing and data reduction. A task-specific request is not a compressed replacement for every original image. Remote compute cannot fix an undersized uplink. When incoming demand exceeds outgoing capacity, backlog grows even with negligible network transit time. A larger buffer only postpones overflow. We can increase connection capacity, send less data, reduce the incoming workload, or keep more processing local. The local PCIe constraint is a separate problem: Gen6 or a second independent Gen5 x16 link doubles that conveyor’s capacity and reduces balanced utilization from 88.6% to 44.3%. Both workflows start with a 384 MB sensor package at 120 packages/s. Producing the 100 kB cloud request takes a 3,840-to-one reduction, and the full 46.08 GB/s still has to reach the local reduction stage. Reads, writes, and intermediate copies can add more memory and interconnect traffic. Placement matters: FPGA-side selection can reduce downstream PCIe demand; GPU-side selection requires the full input to reach the GPU first. The bandwidth saving also carries an information tradeoff. A selected 100 kB request cannot preserve the complete 384 MB image package in this example: cropping can remove scene context, downsampling can reduce spatial resolution, and feature extraction can omit details that a different or future model might need. Lossless compression preserves information, but cannot be assumed to deliver this reduction. The cloud therefore works from a narrower representation, not the same full-resolution input available locally. The design decision is how much local bandwidth and processing to spend on reduction, what sensor detail to retain, and whether the resulting task performance justifies the uplink saving. In factory terms, shipping only selected material relieves the outbound lane, but inspection and sorting still need local capacity—and discarded material is unavailable to the external work center. Section 4: How Do You Manage Bottlenecks When AI Demand Varies? Average capacity is only the first test. Crop density and scene complexity can change inference work or the amount of selected data sent downstream, even when the prepared camera frames remain fixed at 8 MB. Retransmissions, scheduling, and competing devices can change the service available on a PCIe or network path. These variations create uneven demand and service times—and queues that an average bandwidth figure alone cannot describe. With a package arriving every 8.33 milliseconds and a fixed transfer time, Gen5 clears each package before the next one arrives. Barely. Its 7.38-millisecond transfer at 88.6% utilization leaves approximately 0.95 milliseconds of breathing room. Gen6 finishes in 3.69 milliseconds, leaving approximately 4.64 milliseconds. Bursts, competing transfers, and variable service times eat into that margin and force work to wait. Inference is already at 72% and the locally reduced cloud uplink at 80%, so relieving transport can move the traffic jam elsewhere. Add a second independent Gen5 x16 path and a shared queue can send the next complete package to whichever link is free, provided both reach the required destination. Each link supplies approximately 135.4 packages/s; together they provide approximately 270.8 packages/s, with 44.3% balanced utilization at 120 arriving packages/s. Each link is a service resource, not a separate computer. For variable traffic, model that pooled queue as M/M/2: two servers with Poisson arrivals and exponential service times. The synchronized camera stream supplies the regular-arrival baseline; the M/M/2 model addresses random arrivals and variable service. Two Gen5 links, whole-package dispatch: Each package still takes 7.38 milliseconds to transfer, but two packages can move concurrently, reducing contention. One Gen6 link: Each package transfers in 3.69 milliseconds. Two Gen5 links, striped package: Splitting one package evenly across both can also achieve approximately 3.69 milliseconds, but requires concurrent striping and reassembly—not the same whole-package M/M/2 model. Fixed camera assignment: Permanently assigning 24 cameras to each link creates two separate queues rather than one pooled queue. Equal aggregate bandwidth does not mean equal response time. Dispatch policy determines how much of that capacity the workload can actually use. The added conveyor must remain independent through the constrained stage. Two x16 device connections that converge on the same saturated switch uplink do not double end-to-end capacity. Think of an Ethernet switch: feed two sustained wire-speed inputs into a single output of identical bandwidth and twice as much traffic arrives as can leave. The backlog grows past any two-buffer limit, driving L > 2 in the lossless backlog model and triggering backpressure or dropped packets when finite buffers fill. The exact same oversubscription principle applies to PCIe switching, although PCIe uses flow control rather than Ethernet-style congestion drops. Switch bandwidth, endpoint connectivity, memory bandwidth, and downstream accelerator capacity must support the parallel paths. An edge AI platform must therefore be architected as a non-blocking fabric, where aggregate ingress bandwidth never oversubscribes the downstream egress paths to the GPU or host memory. Once transport is relieved, the constraint may move to inference or another work center. The practical design loop is to identify the constraint, add capacity or change dispatch at that stage, and then measure the complete flow again. Safety capacity: the equivalent of safety stock. A factory does not plan inventory only for average demand; it chooses a service level and carries protection against demand above that average. An Edge AI pipeline faces a similar decision. For independent, randomly arriving requests at a steady average rate, a Poisson distribution describes how many may arrive within a given interval. That can model event-triggered jobs or competing requests, rather than the regularly synchronized camera packages in our example. Spare link and accelerator capacity provide the safety margin, while buffers absorb short bursts. Unlike inventory on a shelf, however, a real-time decision expires: extra buffering cannot rescue a result delivered after its deadline. The equivalent of a stockout is a missing, dropped, or late decision. The target is therefore an on-time service level, not simply machine uptime—for example, delivering 99.9% of required decisions before their deadlines over a defined operating period. A demand percentile alone does not establish that result: existing backlog, service times, parallel paths, and the deadline also determine the outcome. Adding a second independent PCIe path becomes a service-level investment, not merely a bandwidth upgrade. The queueing model connects variable demand and available service capacity to the probability of delivering useful work on time. The relevant design target is therefore not simply average bandwidth or average inference time. It is the probability that the complete sensor-to-command path meets its deadline. For a laser-weeding machine, the team should measure median and tail latency, queue depth by stage, dropped or stale frames, retransmissions, and the percentage of targeting decisions delivered before the plant leaves the laser’s effective window. This also changes how optimization work is prioritized. If the PCIe switch uplink limits sustained throughput, increasing GPU throughput alone will not raise the line’s output. For a transport constraint, compare faster links with additional independent x16 paths and the scheduling needed to use them. For a cloud-uplink constraint, compare greater connection capacity with local selection or compression that reduces outgoing demand. Operations management evaluates each improvement against the current throughput constraint, then checks whether the constraint has moved. Meeting the response deadline requires a separate analysis of cumulative latency. Figure 3. One Gen5 x16 path, two pooled independent Gen5 x16 paths, and one Gen6 x16 path offer different transfer times and dispatch options, with inference at 72% utilization becoming a potential next constraint. Section 5: What Does Bottleneck Analysis Change About Edge AI Design? Modeling an Edge AI pipeline as a factory floor changes the question from “Which component is fastest?” to “Which stage limits the complete flow?” A network diagram reveals the handoffs. Capacity analysis exposes the constrained lanes and links. Little’s Law translates delay into work-in-process and buffer demand. Queuing theory explains both the cost of high utilization and the value of parallel service resources. A faster conveyor and a second conveyor are different design choices; topology and dispatch determine which one best protects the flow. For the laser-weeding example, the bandwidth comparison makes the feasible division of work visible. The complete camera array requires 368.64 Gb/s, far beyond the assumed 120 Mb/s cloud uplink. Selecting one 100 kB request per complete package reduces demand to 96 Mb/s, but changes the cloud’s role to processing selected information rather than the full array. This is the shipping-lane constraint: remote processing capacity cannot compensate for a connection that cannot sustain the incoming data rate. The payoff is a different investment decision. With one Gen5 link, transport uses 88.6% of capacity and inference uses 72%. Add an independent Gen5 link or upgrade to Gen6, and transport falls to 44.3%; inference is now the more heavily loaded of those two work centers. The next improvement belongs at the new constraint, not automatically at the newest or fastest component. Bandwidth and latency are different tests. Little’s Law translates flow time into work-in-process; comparing local and cloud response times requires the elapsed time along each complete path. Capture, preparation, transfer, processing, and control add time wherever one step waits for another. Overlapping successive packages can keep throughput high without shortening any individual package’s trip. A factory can hit its production rate and still miss a delivery promise. So can this pipeline. Add up processing, handoffs, waiting, and network delays—and check the slowest responses, not just the average. Both hardware and software determine that result. Hardware supplies the lanes, memory bandwidth, parallel work centers, and connectivity; software determines how work reaches them through scheduling, batching, queue management, data placement, and synchronization. More links cannot help if software funnels every transfer through one path, and better scheduling cannot create bandwidth that the hardware does not provide. Protecting the flow means designing the physical factory and its dispatch rules together. For OSS, that translates into concrete design questions: Do rugged PCIe interconnects and switch fabrics provide independent paths where the workload needs them? Can GPUs, NVMe storage, and high-speed NICs exchange data without avoidable staging? Can the thermal architecture sustain that capacity under real operating conditions? These are not separate specification checks; together, they determine whether the pipeline keeps work moving. The math behind operations management has not changed. The factory floor is now a stream of sensor data moving through lanes, memory, accelerators, networks, and control systems—and the best architecture is the one that protects the flow.

articles.summary: Latest award expands OSS’s role in a next-generation platform for mission-critical electronic warfare simulation Ninth order since May 2025 brings cumulative orders to nearly $5 million, with additional opportunities expected in 2027 and 2028 ESCONDIDO, Calif. – October 8, 2026 – One Stop Systems, Inc. (OSS or the Company) (Nasdaq: OSS), a leader in rugged Enterprise Class compute for artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML) and sensor processing at the edge, today announced that a leading defense and intelligence contractor has placed a new $1 million follow-on production order in support of a next-generation GNSS testing and simulation platform. This is the ninth order from this customer since the relationship began in May 2025 and brings total orders to date to nearly an aggregate $5 million. OSS expects additional opportunities in 2027 and 2028 to support this testing and simulation platform. Under the latest award, OSS will provide its Gen 5 PCIe 4U short-depth server (SDS) as the compute foundation for the customer’s next-generation GNSS simulation platform. The platform is a multi-element, phase-coherent GNSS simulator designed specifically for Controlled Reception Pattern Antenna (CRPA) testing and can simultaneously simulate multiple threats, including jamming, spoofing and repeating. The follow-on award reflects continued expansion of OSS’ role in supporting the customer’s high-fidelity simulation environments for electronic warfare signal processing and complex antenna-array modeling. “We are thrilled to build on this relationship and support the next generation of the customer’s GNSS simulation platform,” said Mike Knowles, President and CEO of OSS. “Being selected again as the program advances from Gen 2 to Gen 3 reflects what we believe is the value of our rugged, Enterprise Class compute architecture and our ability to integrate the latest GPU and CPU technologies into proven edge platforms.” Knowles continued, “We are increasingly seeing initial platform wins develop into recurring production opportunities as customers move from development into deployment. Based on current program expectations, OSS anticipates potential additional orders on this program in 2027 and 2028. We believe it may be another example of the growing base of multi-year platform opportunities we are developing across our defense and commercial markets.” About One Stop SystemsOne Stop Systems, Inc. (Nasdaq: OSS) is a leader in AI enabled solutions for the demanding 'edge'. OSS designs and manufactures Enterprise Class compute and storage products that enable rugged AI, sensor fusion and autonomous capabilities without compromise. These hardware and software platforms bring the latest data center performance to harsh and challenging applications, whether they are on land, sea or in the air. OSS products include ruggedized servers, compute accelerators, flash storage arrays, and storage acceleration software. These specialized compact products are used across multiple industries and applications, including autonomous trucking and farming, as well as aircraft, drones, ships and vehicles within the defense industry. OSS solutions address the overall AI workflow, from high-speed data acquisition to deep learning, training and large-scale inference, and have delivered many industry firsts for industrial OEM and government customers. As one of the fastest growing segments of the multi-billion-dollar edge computing market, AI enabled solutions require-and OSS delivers-the highest level of performance in the most challenging environments without compromise. articles.summary: Disruptive rugged tactical computing platform designed to deliver 600x lower latency and 6x greater bandwidth MOSA-aligned architecture builds on OSS’s deployed Cernis/Donati/Sensor Concentrator lineage to eliminate legacy VPX processing bottlenecks Tamarack-G designed specifically for 360° Situational Awareness, full-spectrum counter UAS, and next-generation communication platforms ESCONDIDO, Calif. – October 12, 2026 – One Stop Systems, Inc. (OSS or the Company) (Nasdaq: OSS), a leader in rugged Enterprise Class compute for artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and sensor processing at the edge, today announced Tamarack-G, a Modular Open Systems Approach (MOSA) aligned OCP/VPX hybrid computing platform. Debuting at the Association of the United States Army (AUSA) 2026 Annual Meeting in Washington, D.C., Tamarack-G bridges legacy VPX infrastructure with data center-class Open Computer Project (OCP) processing density for Denied, Degraded, Intermittent, and Limited-bandwidth (DDIL) environments. OSS will showcase its commercially available Tamarack-G hybrid architecture in Hall D, Booth 7454 at the Walter E. Washington Convention Center from October 12–14, 2026. To schedule an executive or technical briefing, visit www.onestopsystems.com. “With legacy VPX-based computing architectures widely deployed across U.S. and allied military platforms, we believe that the need to modernize these systems to support increasingly demanding AI, sensor processing and autonomous applications has never been greater,” said Mike Knowles, President and CEO of OSS. “Tamarack-G is designed to provide defense customers with a powerful, modular upgrade path that preserves existing infrastructure while dramatically expanding computing performance. By consolidating the capabilities of multiple legacy systems into a single rugged platform, we believe Tamarack-G positions OSS to address a significant modernization opportunity while delivering the mission-critical capabilities required by today's warfighters and tomorrow's ever more sophisticated defense platforms.” Tamarack-G is designed to address the growing need for high-performance computing across new and existing military vehicle platforms. By combining advanced AI processing capabilities with established VPX architectures, the platform enables defense contractors to modernize existing systems, consolidate multiple computing functions and support increasingly complex mission requirements without replacing their entire computing infrastructure. Tamarack-G builds directly on OSS’s proven high-speed compute architecture first introduced in the Company’s ultra-rugged, GPU accelerated Cernis, Donati and Donati-SC vehicle server platforms. By leveraging native PCI Express (PCIe) interconnects directly across vehicle platform subsystems rather than relying solely on traditional Ethernet-switched backplanes, Tamarack-G delivers 600x lower interconnect latency and 6x higher bandwidth moving data, such as uncompressed video, among platform systems. This direct end-to-end PCIe architecture eliminates data ingest and stack processing bottlenecks, allowing multi-sensor fusion engines to process massive data streams in real time. Rather than forcing defense programs into a binary choice between replacing established VPX chassis and sensor investments or sacrificing processing density, Tamarack-G provides a seamless hybrid path. The platform integrates high-density OCP AI/ML Server and enterprise-class GPU accelerated compute modules directly alongside VPX systems, packing enough processing horsepower into a single chassis to consolidate missions that previously required four to five separate VPX systems. A single Tamarack-G system simultaneously executes: 360° Situational Awareness (360-SA) and autonomous navigation processing; Full-spectrum Counter-UAS (C-UAS) detection, tracking, and active/passive countermeasures across radar, EO/IR, RF, audio, and digital broadcast inputs; and Red/Black multi-domain communications to enable real-time vehicle-to-vehicle C-UAS orchestration at the armored platoon level. By maintaining strict alignment with MOSA and SOSA open standards initiatives while embedding enterprise-grade PCIe fabrics, Tamarack-G offers defense integrators and program offices an order-of-magnitude leap in inference performance without requiring a complete, risk-heavy overhaul of existing vehicle infrastructure.
